solutions.latex: The cumulative percentage point at 'Spotty' (the third bar) is $80\%$. Answer (C).
$y=\sqrt{4-x^2}$ is the upper semicircle, so different $x$ values (e.g. $\pm x$) give the same $y$: it is many-to-one. Answer (B).
Reflect in the $y$-axis: $y=(-x)^2+4(-x)+7=x^2-4x+7$. Translate $2$ right: $y=(x-2)^2-4(x-2)+7=(-x+2)^2+4(-x+2)+7$. Answer (B).
$y''$ changes sign about $x=3$ but not about $x=1$ (repeated factor), so the only point of inflection is at $x=3$. Answer (C).
The graph of $f(x)=|6-2x|$ has a sharp point at $x=3$, so it is not differentiable there. Answer (D).
Displacement is the area under the velocity graph; it is a maximum where $v$ changes from positive to negative, at $t=7$. Answer (D).

solutions.latex:
$f'(x)=0$: $1-x^2=0$, so $x=\pm1$. When $x=1$, $y=\dfrac12$; when $x=-1$, $y=-\dfrac12$.

$$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2\\ \hline f'(x) & -\frac{3}{25} & 0 & 1 & 0 & -\frac{3}{25}\end{array}$$

So $\left(1,\tfrac12\right)$ is a local maximum and $\left(-1,-\tfrac12\right)$ is a local minimum (the gradient changes from positive to negative at $x=1$, and from negative to positive at $x=-1$).

solutions.latex:
Area of metal required $A=(2r)^2+2\pi r\times h$.

But $V=\pi r^2h$, i.e. $h=\dfrac{V}{\pi r^2}$.

$A=4r^2+2\pi r\times\dfrac{V}{\pi r^2}=4r^2+\dfrac{2V}{r}$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 2: complete derivation; 1: correct expression for $A$ in $r$ and $h$ / substitution of $h$

solutions.latex:
$\dfrac{dA}{dr}=-\dfrac{2V}{r^2}+8r=0$ when $\dfrac{2V}{r^2}=8r$, so $r^3=\dfrac{V}{4}$.

$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=\dfrac{4V}{r^3}+8=\dfrac{4V\times4}{V}+8=24>0$ (concave up), so we have a local minimum.

The minimum area is $A=4r^2+\dfrac{2V}{r}=\dfrac{4r^3+2V}{r}=\dfrac{3V}{r}=\dfrac{3V}{\sqrt[3]{V/4}}=3\sqrt[3]{4}\,V^{2/3}$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 4: correct answer; 1: correct derivative; 1: $r^3=V/4$; 1: test for minimum; 1: minimum area in terms of $V$

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1295_q32_s1}

The hint gives $x\cos x=\int\cos x\,dx-\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-\int x\sin x\,dx$, hence $\int x\sin x\,dx=\sin x-x\cos x$.

The curves intersect at $x=1$. For $0<x<1$, $\sin x>x\sin x$, so

$A_1=\displaystyle\int_0^1(\sin x-x\sin x)\,dx=\Big[-\cos x-\sin x+x\cos x\Big]_0^1=(-\cos1-\sin1+\cos1)-(-1)=1-\sin1$.

Similarly $A_2=\displaystyle\int_1^{\pi}(x\sin x-\sin x)\,dx=\Big[\sin x-x\cos x+\cos x\Big]_1^{\pi}=(\pi-1)-\sin1$.

Total area $A=A_1+A_2=1-\sin1+\pi-\sin1-1=\pi-2\sin1\approx1.46$ units$^2$.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 4: correct answer; 1: splits area at intersection; 1: correct integrals; 1: correct antiderivative and evaluation; 1: total $\pi-2\sin1\approx1.46$
